steps.body:
A two-way table sorts one group by **two questions at once**. Each of the 200 students lands in exactly one inner cell, so the four inner cells add to 200. The edge totals are just those cells summed along a row or a column.

You met these tables in Grade 8. Now every count in one becomes a probability: divide by the grand total.

explanationVariants: The bus-and-sport cell holds 40 students, and the grand total is 200, so P = 40/200 = 0.20.
20% of the whole class is in that one cell — one cell out of four, but the cells are not equal in size, so you must use its actual count.

widget.prompt: P(takes the bus **and** plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 40/100 — you divided by the bus row instead of the whole group. A joint probability always divides by the grand total, 200.
That is 40/110 — dividing by the sport column. For a joint probability the denominator is everyone: 200.
That is P(bus), the whole row. The question asks for students who are in the bus row AND the sport column: the single cell where they cross.

steps.body:
Two names for two shapes:

**Joint** probability — one inner cell over the total. P(bus and sport) = 40/200.

**Marginal** probability — a whole edge total over the total. P(sport) = 110/200.

Same denominator, different shaded region. Marginals ignore the second question entirely.

explanationVariants: The sport column totals 40 + 70 = 110, so P(sport) = 110/200 = 0.55.
Ignore the travel question completely. Of 200 students, 110 play a sport — that is 55%.

widget.prompt: P(plays a sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the joint cell 40/200 — bus riders who play a sport. The marginal also counts the 70 walkers who play.
That is 70/200, the walkers who play. Add the 40 bus riders who play as well: 110 of 200.
That is 90/200 — the *no sport* column. The two columns are complements, so a slip here flips the event.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Sum the whole sport column: 40 + 70 = 110, so 110/200 = 0.55.

steps.body: One square per student — 200 of them.

widget.prompt: Shade the students who take the bus **and** play a sport.
widget.successFeedback: 40 of 200 squares — one fifth. That single inner cell is the joint probability P(bus and sport) = 0.20.
widget.lowFeedback: Fewer than 40 squares. The bus-and-sport cell holds 40 of the 200 students.
widget.highFeedback: More than 40 squares — that is drifting toward a whole row (100) or column (110), which would be a marginal, not a joint.

predict.prompt: You'll shade 1/5 of the grid. Will that cover more or less than half of it?
predict.reveal: Half means the numerator is half the denominator — 2.5/5 here — and 1 is less. When halving leaves a fraction like 2.5, double the numerator instead and compare: 2 against 5 gives the same verdict with whole numbers. Probability as shaded area makes the benchmark visible before you count a single cell.

cml.actionGoal: Select regions of an equal-outcome sample space and coordinate area with event probability.

explanationVariants: A marginal probability collapses one question away and uses an edge total: P(walks) = 100/200.
Joint statements contain an "and" joining both questions. Marginal statements mention only one of the two questions.

widget.prompt: Which of these is a **marginal** probability?

options.label: P(walks) = 100/200
options.feedback: Right — it uses a whole edge total and says nothing about sport, so one question has been collapsed away.

options.label: P(walks and no sport) = 30/200
options.feedback: Both questions are pinned down, so this is one inner cell: a joint probability.

options.label: P(bus and sport) = 40/200
options.feedback: The "and" is the giveaway — two questions answered at once means one inner cell, which is joint.

options.label: P(sport, among bus riders) = 40/100
options.feedback: That divides by 100, not 200 — it is a conditional probability, restricted to the bus row. That is the next chapter.

steps.body: Match each statement to its fraction.
explanationVariants: Joint statements pick one inner cell; marginal statements pick a whole edge. Every fraction here is over the grand total, 200.
Bus is a row total (100). No-sport is a column total (90). Walks-and-sport is the single cell where that row meets that column (70).

widget.prompt: Match each probability to the count above 200.

pairErrors.feedback: 70 is the walkers who play — one inner cell. P(bus) is the whole bus row: 40 + 60 = 100.
100 is a row total (bus). The no-sport column totals 60 + 30 = 90.

widget.missFeedback: Rows total 100 and 100; columns total 110 and 90; inner cells are 40, 60, 70, 30.
widget.successFeedback: Two edges and one cell — you can now read any joint or marginal probability straight off the table.

hints: You are told a column total and one of the two cells inside it. The column has only two cells.
The no-sport column totals 90, and 30 of those students walk. Everyone else in that column takes the bus.
So the bus-and-no-sport cell holds 90 − 30 = 60. Now divide by the grand total, 200.
explanationVariants: The no-sport column is 90, of which 30 walk, so 60 take the bus. P(bus and no sport) = 60/200 = 0.30.
Work along the bus row instead: it totals 100, and 40 of those play a sport, so 60 do not — the same cell, 60/200 = 0.30.

widget.prompt: You are told only this: 200 students, 90 play no sport, 30 of those 90 walk, and 100 take the bus. Find **P(takes the bus and plays no sport)**.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 60/90 — dividing by the no-sport column. That is a conditional probability; a joint one divides by all 200.
That is 90/200, the marginal P(no sport). The question asks for the bus riders inside that column, which is 90 − 30 = 60.
That is 30/200 — the walkers with no sport. The bus riders in that column are the other 60.

widget.fallbackFeedback: 90 − 30 = 60 bus riders play no sport, so 60/200 = 0.30.

steps.body: One table, two kinds of probability.
takeaways: Joint = one inner cell ÷ grand total. It answers both questions at once.
Marginal = one edge total ÷ grand total. It ignores the other question.
Every cell and every edge shares the same denominator, so the four inner cells sum to 1.
steps.teaser: Next: what changes when the denominator stops being everybody.

concept.body: A joint probability answers **both** questions at once, so it lives in a single inner cell — never a row, never a column. Its denominator is always the grand total, because the student could have landed anywhere in the table.

explanationVariants: Walks and no sport is the bottom-right inner cell: 30 students out of 200, so 0.15.
The walk row is 100 and 70 of them play, leaving 30 who do not — 30/200 = 0.15.

widget.prompt: From the same table: P(walks **and** plays no sport). Give a decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 30/100 — dividing by the walk row. A joint probability divides by everyone: 200.
That is the whole no-sport column, 90/200. Only the walkers inside it count here: 30.
